speechtext:
that Bill C-24, an Act to amend certain legislation respecting superannuation and other pensions, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to introduce the second reading of Bill C-24, a Bill that proposes to remove from a number of Public Service superannuation laws, the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act and the Pension Act as it applies to disabled veterans, certain restrictions on survivors' benefits based on age and marital status.
First of all, I would like to point out that the tabling of this Bill at the beginning of the second session of Parliament testifies to the Government's sustained interest in and commitment to the reform of our pension legislation.

Bill C-24, entitled the Statute Law (Superannuation) Amendment Act, would amend the superannuation plans for federal public servants, members of the armed forces and the RCMP, certain non-career diplomats and Members of Parliament. It would also amend certain provisions of the Pension Act which apply to disabled veterans. Because the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Merrithew) will speak to the effects of this Bill on veterans' pensions, I will confine my remarks to the changes the Bill proposes for the Public Service plans.
The first change proposed under the Bill would remove the provisions which suspend or terminate a surviving spouse's allowance in the event that the surviving spouse remarries. Removing this provision would confer lifetime entitlement to a survivor's pension on an eligible recipient.
Second, the Bill removes in four of the Public Service plans provisions calling for a reduction in the amount of a surviving spouse's pension when a survivor is 20 or
Superannuation
more years younger than the plan member. Third, the Bill removes the provisions which disentitled the child of a deceased plan member to a student allowance if the student is married after reaching age 18.
A fourth change which has very limited application removes the provision under the RCMP Pension Continuation Act and the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act that a son's entitlement ceases at age 18 whereas an unmarried daughter retains benefits until age 21. The Bill provides that the children's benefits continue until age 21 regardless of marital status.

Under these pension plans, some surviving spouses elected, when they remarried, to receive a lump sum instead of having their benefits suspended. Since these benefits will now be reinstated, the lump sums paid will have to be paid back to the pension fund accounts. I can assure Hon. Members that everything will be done to ensure that the reimbursement process is handled with sensitivity and compassion. We would like to see the regulations provide for a reimbursement process similar to that being used now to recover overpayments from other survivors. This means that 10 per cent of the reinstated pension would be collected to pay for the lump sum payment, and there would be no extra charges. However, individuals may opt to increase or decrease this percentage, depending on their financial circumstances.
The Government estimates that about 2,200 surviving spouses will benefit from the elimination of the provision on remarriage which was part of the Public Service plans. The other changes will affect a smaller number of people. There may be as many as 500 surviving spouses receiving reduced benefits on the basis of an age difference of 20 years or more. The Government estimates that the additional benefit payments to be paid annually as a result of these changes will total $11 million.
Mr. Speaker, I believe all Hon. Members will be pleased to hear that the Bill provides, as of the effective date of the legislation, for the reinstatement of suspended or reduced benefits in the case of individuals who were affected by these provisions. I would like to point out to the House that those responsible for operating the pensions plans in question will make every effort to find every individual whose benefits were

On a final note, I am aware that there are number of outstanding and important pension issues which need to be addressed in the public service plans. Agreement on some of these matters has already been reached with plan members, while other matters need further consultation. subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise this morning to extend my compliments to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) for doing the honourable thing for the widows, widowers, and children of federal pensioners.
After four long years, he has managed to overcome the inertia of his Government and table a Bill that is a first step toward bringing federal pensions in line with the equality provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. At last, the survivors of those who worked for the people of Canada will not have to choose between "living in sin" to continue receiving income they relied on for their retirement years, or remarrying and forgoing a pension to which they are entitled.
In 1985, the report Equality for All recommended that federal superannuation legislation be amended to remove the discriminatory provisions that offended Section 15 of the Charter, on the basis of marital status, gender or age.
Specifically, the report recommended the repeal of provisions terminating pension benefits for a surviving spouse who remarried, for surviving children who married, or reducing pensions to survivors more than 20 years younger than the pensioner, the so-called "sugar daddy" clause. These are the recommendations the Bill before us today finally implements.
In its response to the report in 1986 entitled Towards Equality, the Government stated that it was studying these amendments as part of the public service pension reform process then taking place. In fact, for other pensioners, it did implement those changes. The Canada Pension Plan was amended effective January 1,1987, and the Pension Benefits Standards Act of December 1985 covering agencies under federal jurisdiction also ensured the continuation of benefits upon remarriage.
Yet when the report on public service pension reform was tabled by the Minister in June 1986, it left the discriminatory features in federal superannuation legislation for future consideration by a yet non-existent pension management board. Future consideration may be acceptable in trading hockey players. It is not acceptable when dealing with people's livelihoods.
The next stage in this saga was the introduction of the infamous Bill C-33 to reform public service pension legislation. It removed guaranteed indexing from federal pension plans, but did nothing to remove glaring inequities based on marital status, gender, and age. That Bill died on the Order Paper two years later as the Government faced an election and the wrath of a quarter of a million public service employees across Canada.
In bringing forward this Bill today for second reading, the Minister is doing more than correcting contraventions of the Charter. He is also saving the taxpayers of Canada a very hefty legal bill. Lest anyone believe that this Bill is motivated by a new spirit of generosity or concern for the deprivation of widows, widowers, and children of federal pensioners, let me draw the attention of the House to the more likely motivation. A court case was launched on April 13 of this year by the Federal Superannuates National Association.
The association has applied to the Federal Court of Canada for a declaration that the termination of pension benefits based on marital status is unconstitutional. In the case of the particular plaintiff, the application seeks reinstatement of the pension, reimbursement of lost

pension benefits, costs, and "such further and other relief as the honourable court deems just".
The Minister has moved wisely and quickly to avoid a lengthy legal battle that would be both costly to the Government, embarrassing, and could have had even more far-reaching results than the Bill before the House today. A guarantee of fairness is an essential element of a good pension plan. Bill C-24 is a long awaited and positive step in that direction.
No one can disagree that those changes are necessary, long overdue, and deserve to be passed without delay. After so many years of inaction, surviving family members are finally getting the benefits to which they have been entitled for so long. They are finally being treated with fairness and without discrimination.
Another change which may not elicit as much attention, but is nonetheless welcome, is the removal of gender based language in the Acts. The law will now recognize that pensioners and survivors may be either men or women, that a child may be either a son or a daughter, and should be treated equally regardless. It will recognize that even Senators-heaven forbid-may be survived by a spouse who is not necessarily a widow.
However, I have several concerns I wish to raise which prevent me from heaping too much praise. First, there is no retroactivity provision in the Bill before us. Benefits will be reinstated from the day the Act comes into force with no compensation provisions for the time benefits were suspended. This means that a surviving spouse, regardless of whether he or she was without benefits for 20 months or 20 years, will get no restitution for past injustices.
Conversely, where a lump sum payment was arranged for survivors in lieu of ongoing benefits, that money will have to be entirely repaid either in a lump sum or by regular monthly deductions, again with no compensation for how long the discriminatory effect was experienced.
I have sought and received the assurances of the Minister, and I am pleased to hear them repeated today, that the regulations to be introduced will allow beneficiaries a wide choice of how they can make the repay-
Superannuation
ment, so that it will not be an onerous obligation, eating away at their restored income.
There are other inequities that still need to be addressed, including the status of common law spouses, discrimination based on age at the time of marriage, and different levels of benefits among different groups of pensioners.
Another essential to survivors' benefits pension reform is the one basic, long awaited change, still unfulfilled-an increase in benefits. Survivors of superannuants in Crown corporations have, for several years now, enjoyed an increase in their pensions to 60 per cent while those of federal pensioners still receive only 50 per cent.
This can perhaps be likened to the story of the shoemaker who provides customers with high quality footwear and careful service while the employees work barefoot. It is all too easy to be cynical about this omission and to believe that the Government is holding this basic entitlement back as a bargaining chip for future pension reform measures which may not be as well received.
If the world were a predictable place with all trends, economic and otherwise, following a clearly defined pattern, then pension plans would be relatively simple and non-contentious. However, many of us in this House know all too well that things do not always go the way we expect them to go. Pension plans by their very definition are the means to guaranteeing a secure future for ourselves and our families when we retire.
Given the unpredictability of our world, this process involves a delicate balance of understanding past trends and educated crystal ball gazing, all the while keeping in mind the best interests of all the contributors and remembering that they have bought and paid for the benefits accrued from their investment. Certain guarantees must be built into any plan to ensure it does not become simply a forced saving with no worth-while investment value. Thus I would like to reiterate some basic principles which must be guarded jealously in future pension reform.
First, the terms "indexed" and "pension" can never be far apart in a discussion of pension reform. We in the

June 22, 1989

Official Opposition believe that an unindexed pension is no pension at all. Without indexation the investment value is simply an illusion for contributors.
Second, the federal pension plan must be credited with a rate of return at least comparable to the best managed private pension plan. This is not the case now. Existing rights and benefits must not be forfeited in exchange for equity and return on investment.
Last, the pension fund must be managed jointly by the employer and the contributors. This will ensure the recognition that all parties "own" the fund.
Bill C-42 is a positive first step on the long road to federal pension reform. I commend the employees and the pensioners for their persistence in seeking equity. I also commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for his unwavering support of their cause, and the Minister for acting before the courts forced it upon him.
However, I must remind the House that this is an area in which the Government has a long way to go towards properly providing for its own employees. The shoemakers are far from taking proper responsibility for their employees and for paying proper attention to the needs, wants, and working conditions of their workers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, it is a pleasure to speak in a positive manner from the opposition benches on this Bill. The Government is to be commended for bringing forward these long overdue provisions to ensure that surviving spouses are included.
This long overdue reform restores benefits to about 6,700 surviving spouses of public servants whose benefits have been discontinued upon their remarriage. Reform to survivors' benefits is especially important to women in Canada. Some 60 per cent of women in Canada aged 65 and older live below the poverty line. A majority of these women, approximately 70 per cent, live their final years alone. The reality is that women are most often the recipients of survivor benefits, and women have the most need for legislation to protect those benefits.
In its 1985 report, the parliamentary committee on equality rights recommended the repeal of the provisions of the Canada Pension Plan and federal superannuation plans which required the termination of benefits to surviving spouses upon remarriage, and the reduction of benefits for survivors 20 or more years younger than the deceased contributor. To terminate benefits for survivors who remarried and to reduce benefits for survivors more than 20 years younger than their spouses clearly discriminated on the basis of marital status and age in violation of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In its response to its report the Government indicated that these changes would be introduced to the Canada Pension Plan to take effect in January 1987, and that they would be studied in the course of the public service pension reform process. It has been almost four years since the committee on equality rights first tabled its report, and more than a year since the recommended changes were introduced to the Canada Pension Plan. While the reforms contained in Bill C-24 are certainly welcome, we must not forget the frustrating period of delay which preceded the introduction of this Bill.
The frustrations of the delay prompted action. In April of this year the Federal Superannuates National Association, which represents 250,000 Canadians who receive federal pensions, launched a Charter challenge based upon discriminatory provisions of the survivors' benefits legislation. The FSNA should be congratulated for its hard work on behalf of federal superannuates and for launching a challenge which provided an impetus for the legislation now before the House.
It is important to note, however, that in the statement of claim filed with the challenge, the federal superannuates asked not only for reinstatement of survivor benefits which had been terminated upon remarriage but also for full payments of all benefits lost as a result of the disentitlement. I refer specifically to the case in the Federal Court of Canada, Trial Division, Nona Horswill v. Her Majesty The Queen in the right of Canada.
In the statement of claim, specifically paragraph 8(d), judgment for such amount of the annual allowance as the plaintiff has not received as a result of the payment having been suspended is asked for. In other words, in that particular case retroactivity is being asked for. Bill C-24 makes no provision for such retroactivity. If we are to recognize the entitlement of remarried survivors to future benefits following the passage of this legislation,
June 22, 1989

we must also recognize their entitlement to past benefits denied by the present legislation.
It is disappointing that the Bill does not provide retroactive payment of benefits. It is also disappointing that the Bill does not address the other issues of concern to federal superannuates.
Another recommendation of the parliamentary committee on equality rights was to repeal the provisions of federal superannuation plans disentitling surviving spouses to benefits when the marriage took place after the contributor's retirement or, in the case of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Forces Superannuation Acts, after the contributor reached 60 years of age. Again, these provisions are clearly contrary to the Charter, I would suggest. Where survivor benefits are provided, they should be available regardless of the date of marriage.
Bill C-24 does nothing to adjust the rate of survivor benefits. Amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act, which took effect in January 1987, require the provisions of survivor benefits equal to at least 60 per cent of the contributor's retirement benefit. While the Canada Pension Plan was amended to reflect this requirement, federal superannuation plans provided a survivor benefit equal to only 50 per cent of the contributor's retirement pension. It is time that the Government brought federal superannuation plans in to line with the Pensions Benefits Act.
Further, this legislation does not address the plight of common law spouses. Some superannuation plans allow Treasury Board full discretion in awarding a survivor benefit to a common law spouse. This means that a survivor benefit may be denied to a common law spouse of a contributor, even where there is no other person claiming to be the spouse.
As required by the PBS A, superannuation legislation must be amended to recognize common law relationships. Both common law and legal marriage must be fully recognized as giving rise to spousal pension rights, such as the splitting of pension credits and entitlement to survivor benefits.
The splitting of pension credits is another important issue which must be addressed. Ex-service wives are especially disadvantaged by the present discriminatory provisions of the Canadian Forces superannuation plan.
Superannuation
Ex-service wives often find themselves in situations of dire poverty even if their ex-spouses agree to full diversion of pension credits. Unlike the PBSA, there are no provisions currently in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act to enable a splitting of pension credits to take place upon marriage breakdown.
The wives of Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel may also find themselves without a survival benefit upon the death of their spouse because the original legislation did not provide for survivor benefits.
While a separate fund was established to allow members of the RCMP to contribute to the provisions of the survivor benefits, there is no mechanism to provide survivor benefits to the survivors of RCMP members who either did not pay into the fund or who withdrew their contributions to the fund.
While the Pension Benefits Standards Act covers workers in federally regulated industries throughout Canada, the largest federal employer in the country, the federal Government, is yet exempt from its provisions. The PBSA deals with important pension issues, including portability, vesting, locking in, pension splitting upon divorce, and early retirement. Treasury Board has responsibility to address these issues in any superannuation legislation it introduces.
The PBSA requires that both full-time workers have access to pension plans after two years of employment, and part-time workers with earnings above $9,000 per year. The right of workers to participate in a pension plan is an important right which must be fully protected. However, all workers should be entitled to participate in a pension plan regardless of their annual level of earnings.
The PBSA requires that benefits be vested after two years participation in a pension plan. Government has a responsibility to ensure that employers honour their pension obligations by vesting pension benefits. The vesting provisions of the PBSA are important ones which must be thoroughly applied to public service pensions.
Bill C-33, which died on the Order Paper in the last session of Parliament, was to address some of these issues by establishing a joint pension management board. However, Bill C-33 empowered Treasury Board to override the decision of the board. It also included the

June 22, 1989
Superannuation
abolition of guaranteed indexing for public service pensions.
Reform of public service pensions is long overdue. Reform must address all of these issues through a system of joint management with equal representation from employees, present retirees, and management. However, it must make no attempt to deny or withhold full and guaranteed pension indexing for all present and future public service superannuants. On the whole this Bill before the House is desirable, but in my remarks I have attempted to show some of the matters we should look at in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not my intention to hold up unduly the debate and timely passage of this Bill today, but I want to thank my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), and indeed all my colleagues for their co-operation in ensuring that a number of spouses of veterans will also benefit from this welcome legislation.
The House will know that pensions are paid to veterans and their survivors as compensation for death and disability incurred during wartime service or as compensation for the time spent as a prisoner of war. As is the custom in a number of programs, remarriage causes surviving spouses to forfeit ongoing pension rights. In the case of our veterans, we are more generous in that we give a one year lump sum to the surviving spouse before the pension is terminated. Of course, this was a special privilege awarded to survivors of that very special group of Canadians, our veterans.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments made to the Pension Act by Bill C-24 will not only help surviving spouses but will also protect the pension rights of children, brothers and sisters under 25 who choose to marry.

We estimate that an average number of 100 surviving spouses of pension veterans remarry each year. In addition, those who have lost their pension over the years through remarriage will, of course, be eligible to apply for reinstatement. We estimate there are some 4,500 surviving spouses in this position. Once this legislation is passed we will do everything we can to let them know the good news. We estimate the cost to be approximately $28 million annually.
In conclusion, I very much the appreciate the co-operative gesture that has been made by both opposition Parties so that we will have swift passage of this piece of important legislation. It will certainly give great comfort to our veterans and indeed to other retired members of the Public Service.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. As was just said, an Opposition Member does not often have the opportunity to say that legislation under consideration is good, that we support it without any reservation and that for once the Government is presenting legislation that we think corrects existing inequities in the laws and that perhaps it should have made these corrections years ago.
I think this Bill C-24, after too much delay, rectifies some discriminatory sections in the pension legislation.
Mr. Speaker, the allowances now paid to surviving spouses of government pensioners, whether they were Public Service employees, veterans, Members of Parliament, Senators or members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, cease when they remarry; allowances paid to surviving children aged 18 to 25 who are students cease when they (re)marry.
In some cases, the allowances paid to the surviving spouse are reduced if the surviving spouse is more than 20 years younger than the contributor. The Bill before us corrects these inequities. Bill C-24 eliminates these sections. Allowances will continue to be paid to a surviving spouse who remarries. Surviving children aged 18 to 25 who are full-time students in a school or university continue and will continue to receive the allowances to which they are entitled, even if they marry.

And third, the allowances will not be reduced for surviving spouses who are more than 20 years younger than the contributor.
Mr. Speaker, I find it somewhat unfortunate, though, that the Government did not choose to bring in these amendments at the same time that it presented a similar law which we passed in 1987, Bill C-88 for the surviving spouses of judges. As we know, the Bill resulted from a recommendation of the Guthrie Commission in 1986, whose mandate was to study the salaries and benefits of judges.
In this report-and to clarify somewhat the Minister's statement that the Government is making this amendment as part of an overall plan, let us say frankly that constitutional considerations forced the Government to meet its obligations. I just want to quote a paragraph of the Guthrie Report: failure to amend the Judges Act (judges were the issue, but it can apply to federal civil servants) to permit continuation of survivors' benefits upon remarriage may raise serious legal questions involving equality rights. We therefore recommend the repeal of subsections 25(3) and 25(3.1) of the Judges Act.
Mr. Speaker, that is what the Government did. In my opinion, what was good for the judges, as I said in the debate then, is also good for public servants, military people, RCMP officers and all the other servants of the state who I think were considered second class citizens, because nothing was done for them.
That being said, I am for passing this Bill because it will finally bring our laws into line with section 15 (of the Charter) and also satisfy the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee in Towards Equality, a report published in 1985 on the subject. I will not read all the recommendations, but anyone interested can refer to the document. It contains a whole series of recommendations that the Government bring the pension legislation into line with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which took effect, as we know, in 1985.
Superannuation
I shall come back to that shortly, because I think that the Government was at fault in refusing to make it retroactive to the proclamation of the Charter in 1985.
Mr. Speaker, on examining these pension plans, we see many deficiencies, inconsistencies and rather disturbing features still in the legislation.
I admit that the Minister told us that a more thorough and complete study of pensions would be done and that more comprehensive legislation might be presented in the fall.
I would like to draw to the attention of Members my preoccupation, and that of some of my colleagues on this side of the House, with certain other laws before us today to be amended in regard to re-marriage and the rights of the children of a married pensioner. There is a section entitled Pension de retraite des Forces canadiennes. I guess it is called The Armed Forces Superannuation Act or some wording of that nature.

Clause 33 contains provisions which I find absolutely unacceptable, Mr. Speaker.
In the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act- [English]
I will read the Superannuation Act concerning military personnel, Section 31(1), because I think this is something that Members will want to correct. Section 31(1) deals with marriage after 60 years of age.
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, the surviving spouse of a person is not entitled to any annual allowance under this Act if that person was over sixty years of age at the time of his marriage, unless, after that time, that person became or continued to be a contributor.
Another section that bothers me, Section 31(2), says:
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, except as provided in the regulations a child who was bom to or adopted by a person or who became the stepchild of a person at a time when that person was over sixty years of age is not entitled to any annual allowance under this Act, unless, after that time, that person became or continued to be a contributor.

June 22, 1989
Superannuation
Those two amendments are required to get away from these regressive and absolutely unacceptable Sections which fly in the face of constitutional rights that Canadians have.
Section 15, as we all know, came into force in 1985. Yet today we have a Bill that says that one could discriminate because of age, or marital status, and discriminate even though a person may be 60 years old and have a child from a marriage following retirement or following the death of the eligible contributor. However that child is not entitled to receive any benefits of the pension.
I believe that the Minister should really look at the possibility of amending that Act when it comes before us. There are divorce laws in this country. We have in Ontario the Family Law Reform Act which deals with separation. Any obligation incurred to support the children remains. In the Divorce Act of Canada it is mandatory that both parents contribute to maintenance, according to each person's ability to pay. The obligation cannot be wiped out. Every relevant piece of legislation that I looked up, for every province, has as a prerequisite that the best interest of the child is of paramount concern. As it should be. Why do we allow inequities to stay on the Statutes of Canada? We know that in some provinces there are laws dealing with the Family Law Reform Act, et cetera. Yet inequities are still maintained.
I would like to ask the Minister to look at all these pension laws. I focused on only a few here because I did not have enough time to research the whole spectrum of pension entitlements. But I know that when the Government came before the House in 1985 with amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act, they corrected all those things for Crown corporations. It made sure that the 60 per cent entitlement to pensions for the spouse was included. We still do not have that for the Public Service, the RCMP or the Armed Forces, et cetera.
I am saying to the Government, if we all accept that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into force in 1985, why not allow retroactivity for those who were hurt, possibly severely, through no fault of their own, by a lack of concern on the part of the employer? Why do we not allow rectroactivity to at least start with the adoption of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in 1985. It would not seem to me to be veiy costly, to be
somewhat considerate and understanding of the need to go back and provide retroactivity.
I have correspondence from the Superannuation Association. I have letters that I could read to the House concerning people who have lived through these difficult situations. For example, I have a letter here from a pensioner who tells me that if he lived common law, he would have been able to transfer his entitlement to his surviving spouse. However if he marries, no, he is not entitled to it. It does not make any sense. So let us look at these things and make sure that we deal with them in the Fall.
I just want to touch on one last item. Because of the aging population of Canadians, a lot of people in Canada have federal pensions. They will go to their lawyer and the lawyer will say, "Give me power of attorney over your pension in case you fall sick, or need some assistance, or need to have some expenditures looked after while you are indisposed." You cannot do that in this country. A lawyer cannot have a power of attorney over a federal pensioner's pension. There are arguments for and against, but I think we need to have a debate in this House because our population is aging and we need to look at the rights of these people. Perhaps we should have less bureaucracy and more understanding as to what we can allow in terms of having pensioners give power of attorney to their lawyers, such lawyers as they trust and who would operate under professional standards.
Having said all that, I congratulate the Government for its effort on the question of Bill C-24, wanting to correct some anomalies and some inequities. There are still lots of things to do. We have done a bit. We have gone a short way down the road toward parity, equity and justice, but we have a long way to go yet on many of these Bills before we reach equity and justice for all Canadians who receive pensions from the federal Government.

June 22, 1989
Museums MUSEUMS ACT
The House resumed from Thursday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Masse that Bill C-12, an Act respecting museums, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak in favour of Bill C-12 which restructures the national museums of Canada into four autonomous arm's length corporations.
Museums are important to our society. They are vital institutions which remind us of where our society has come from and which shed light on where we are going. They are our collective memory with a broad appeal that most do not realize.
As the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) stated just two weeks ago at the parliamentary committee, more people attend museums in Canada than professional sporting events. He stated that 20 million Canadians visit museums. Unfortunately, he is a bit behind in his figures.
According to Statistics Canada many more visit our museums and related institutions. In fact, there are over 90 million visitors each year. Even the Minister's predecessor, Flora MacDonald, was aware of this figure when she spoke just a year ago at the Cultural Tourism Conference in Montreal.
Museums are more than just statistics and people going through turn-stiles. The real impact is on our appreciation and awareness of our society as a multicultural society. As we enter free trade with the United States, we need more than ever institutions which reinforce our sense of place, being and community. That is the unique role of museums. I know this because I have had the opportunity to work in this field. In the mid-1970s, I worked on Canada's Discovery Train, a travelling museum which demonstrated our rich and diverse cultures.
Today, museums in this critical period of our history face enormous challenges to serve a diverse, complex and growing audience. I have a vision of the museum world of the year 2000 which is vibrant, rich and accessible to a broad public, not a limited few.
There has never been a more significant need for museums and for the services they provide, from partnerships with public schools to outreach, to non-traditional museum goers, and to the incredible opportunities to develop exhibitions, collections and educational programs that reflect the depth and variety of our cultural experiences. We have the chance to see museums greatly enrich our society in ways never before experienced.
This is the challenge facing us, both in restructuring the federal museums through this Bill and also in implementing a new federal museums policy to which the Government has committed itself. This a time of change arid it is time to assist these important institutions in their service to our society.
As Dr. Louis Lemieux, former Director of the National Museum of Natural Sciences in Ottawa stated: "Museums, as traditionally defined as institutions devoted to the procurement, care, and display of objects of lasting interest of value, are outdated and inadequate."
Today, we have the opportunity to permit our museums to grow and to serve a wider public, as well as to preserve and study our collections. Bill C-12, and the proposals for a new museums policy will encourage growth.
The first museum in the world was a government institution. It was part of the palace of King Ptolemy in Alexandria which, in the 3rd century B.C., housed the library of Alexander the Great. It was called by the Greek term museion or temple of the muses and was the world's chief centre for learning in its day.
In the centuries that have elapsed since the founding of the Museum of Alexandria, the concepts of what a great museum should be and what it should do have undergone many changes. Fundamentally, a museum is still an institution, not only for collecting and preserving objects, but also for the study of them and the use of them for education and enjoyment.
Almost 1,200 years after the Alexandria Museum was destroyed by war, the National Museum of Canada had its beginnings. In 1842 the geological survey of Canada was established in Montreal and grew into our National Museum in Ottawa. Incidentally, the New Brunswick Museum in Saint John was started in the same year in the Mechanics Institute. From those early starts, museums in Canada have grown steadily so that we virtually
June 22, 1989

now have museums in every community in the country. There are now almost 2,000 museums and related institutions in Canada.
The national museums had precarious beginnings. Indeed, their whole history has been marginal. They have been switched among government Departments, placed in basements or ill-suited buildings, and even in condemned buildings.
In 1981 the then Prime Minister Trudeau announced that proud new homes would be built for two of our national museums, the National Gallery and the Canadian Museum of Civilization. These are the first properly designed homes for these institutions in their histories. For the first time these museums will receive professionally acceptable storage facilities for their multi-million dollar collections and will also be properly displayed. The new home for the National Aviation Museum is also a reality.
Sadly the other national collections remain in inadequate facilities. The National Museum of Science and Technology is in an old bakery, and the Museum of Natural Science is relegated to half of the Victoria Memorial Building, as well as 13 other locations throughout the National Capital Region. The War Museum has actually lost 40,000 square feet of space, and its needs are legendary.
Bill C-12 will not solve those problems, but it will start a process of greater direct control over the management of these important treasures. It will give them far more independence from government, will reduce bureaucracies, and will permit them to retain the funds that they raise. These directions are consistent with many studies, including the task force led by Clement Richard and William Withrow. As well, the Canadian Museums Association held a series of regional meetings in 15 locations which concurred with the Richard-Withrow recommendations. Further, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture supported those recommendations in its unanimous report of January 1987.
The restructuring of the National Museums by Bill C-12 is essentially a housekeeping Bill, but it will result in more efficient operations in their own destiny and guided by their own missions. I am pleased to see the mandates of the museums articulated in this legislation.
Museums
However, I am disappointed that the Government has not yet moved on the other half of reforming museums policy for the rest of the country. The National Museums are all located in Ottawa. I firmly believe the Government has a role in assisting the other museums across Canada. In 1987 the former Minister, Flora MacDonald, pledged that a new policy would be developed. Extensive and extended consultations were held, but the Government has not yet introduced this broader policy, nor has it honoured its commitment to even increase funding by some $2 million saved from the Mobile Exhibits Program.
The grants program for museums has remained static since 1972. The Museum Assistance Program remains unchanged, even for inflation, at $8.5 million. I cannot think of a more neglected yet deserving program. These funds are returned to government via taxes from the economic stimulation created by millions of visitors who attend museums each year in Canada. That is a great return on our investment, but one that I believe can be improved even more.
Our museums, art galleries, historic sites, and science centres contain millions of objects, and for every object there is a fascinating story. We need to tell these stories to more people. Because budgets are so tight in museums, little to no money is available for proper marketing. More money needs to be made available. Other government agencies should become involved such as tourism and the CBC. The rationale for having culture located within the Department of Communications is to see more cultural programming on television, in films, etc.
When was the last time someone saw a show about our museums? On Tuesday, officials of the National Gallery told the parliamentary committee that they approached the CBC to do a show on the gallery at the time of its opening last spring. The CBC declined.
Canada's heritage is not all in Ottawa. It is located in every part of this country. We need a new vision and a new concept so that our national heritage abounds in all museum collections. The artefacts of the Campbell River Museum in British Columbia and of the Yarmouth Firefighters' Museum in Nova Scotia are part of our national patrimony, as are the great collections in the National Gallery.
Finally, I would like to salute the thousands of volunteers across Canada who contribute their time and energy to preserving our great resources of cultural heritage. I make one last plea for greater marketing

support to promote these museums across Canada. I believe that the Government is missing an even greater return on this existing investment because of its attitude toward its lack of marketing support.

speechtext: On debate, the Hon. Member for Mission-Coquitlam.

Mr. Speaker, today, museums are cutting back on people in the same manner as many other areas of our society. Museums are about our culture and about our achievements. People should be very much a part of our museums. Without people, museums are very much a graveyard of our society. It takes people to bring museums alive. They should be vibrant places of our culture, our history, and places that look to our future.
Exhibits should not only be displays, especially in the areas of science and technology. Items that have been used by generations of Canadians or by generations of peoples around the world should be displayed in such a manner that we can feel them, touch them, and try them, particularly with our new technology. Machines are not made to be looked at. Machines are made to be used and to be handled. Our museums need to reflect those human touches, and for that we need funding and a commitment to the human element in our society.
Many museums remove the human element by having free days on a Thursday or a Tuesday, without consultation with the community or without consideration of when people work and when people are free to attend museums. Therefore, museums are further restricted particularly to those people who cannot afford to go to a museum and would like to have their children exposed to
our culture. Those people need access. Museums have to reflect and consult with the community in terms of accessibility, including those museums located in Ottawa. There is a movement in France which is trying to put people back into museums. It is one which we should be looking at in Canada and trying to emulate.
Free trade has further attacked our culture and our industries. With them already under attack and with museums being a reflection of our culture, then are not museums under attack, too? Some museums are just for a tiny minority of people. They really are not a great reflection of our culture. For example, many museums do not have displays celebrating the labour movement in Canada, which movement helped to make the country what it is today.
Many museums do not have displays which reflect the ethnocultural nature of Canada. Many museums do not have displays which celebrate the environment.
Our museums need to reflect the true strata of Canada, its peoples, the environment and the assets which make Canada great.
In an independent study of the museums' workforce it was found that there are two major sources of inequality that are closely interdependent in the museums. It comes down to who staffs our museums. Museums are gender-based and institutionalized-based organizations with great differentiations in the labour force. Simply put, women make substantially less money working for museums than do men. We have checked and found this to be true even after the major alternate explanations of income differences, controls and all of the other factors are taken into account. In other words, significant income differences remain between the sexes even after education and experience levels are held constant.
Although there are virtually identical over-all labour force participation rates for men and women, over 70 per cent of employees in the relatively disadvantaged and smaller institutions are women. When the Government moved to dismantle or reorganize the largest, most advantaged museums, we learned that those women who had achieved senior positions were, in many cases, shut out of significant positions in the new structure. New Democrats have raised concerns about equality in our cultural institutions for many years. Our national mu-
June 22, 1989

seums have a very poor record, a record which may now indeed be improving but at a disappointingly slow pace.
If I can use the analogy that museums reflect our history, surely their management practices should reflect our present and our future.
The new Museum of Civilization is geared up with many new staff for its opening later this summer. Roughly one-half of its employees are women. However, only four of the 15 top jobs are held by women. It is very hard to believe that there are only four women in Canada who have the qualifications to aspire to and expect to sit in those top jobs. In the same museum we find women in the traditional roles, the pink collar ghetto, but only 26 per cent of the scientific and professional category with average earnings in excess of $35,000 are women. Some 86 per cent of the administrative support jobs with an average salary hovering around $20,000 are filled by women. I think it is absolutely vital that we consider these figures and think about what our policies should be, not only for museums but when it comes to funding these organizations.
It is important that I include here thanks to the museum for so promptly providing me with these figures.
I invite the Government to review these concerns regarding museums and to report to the legislative committee studying this Bill on its plans for remedy.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-12 before the House today arises from a recommendation made by the task force responsible for examining federal museum policy, a committee chaired by Clement Richard and William Withrow.
I had the honour and the privilege of knowing the director, the former Secretary General of the Corporation, Mr. Leo Dorais, who at the time objected very strongly to this recommendation, claiming that administrative costs were twice as high as they would be if the task were delegated to the four main museums.
Museums
Mr. Dorais made his mark with his very substantial contribution to the National Museums of Canada as their administrator. Mr. Dorais has served Canada and the National Museums well.
We have now reached a new phase.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak in this debate because of the very strong connection with the riding I represent, Ottawa-Vanier. As you know, the National Gallery of Canada is in Ottawa-Vanier. I also have the honour and the privilege of representing several other museums that come under either the National Museum of Natural Sciences or the Canadian Museum of Civilization, and we are very proud of them.
Mr. Speaker, although I am in favour of independent museums, I am also concerned about what will happen to language equality in those museums. It is an issue I certainly want to raise today, and I take this opportunity, since the Minister is here, to ask him once more to give us the assurance that the policies on language of service and language of work will be maintained, even if the museums are decentralized and even if each museum becomes an autonomous entity.
Mr. Speaker, official languages have never been a priority for our museums. A special report submitted by the Commissioner of Official Languages shows that French takes second place in active offers of service. In fact, according to the Commissioner's report, security staff was unilingual and French information material was inadequate. In some museums, publications in French were more expensive, sometimes as much as twice or three times the price of the same publication in English.
As far as language of work is concerned, the situation is even worse. In fact, there is no option. The report shows that English is the only language of work and that in professional circles, Francophones have to draft their reports in English to be understood by their superiors.
The National Museums Corporation took a step in the right direction by signing an agreement with Treasury Board. Now we must make sure the agreement continues to be applied in each museum.
Only the Secretary General, Mr. Edwards, was accountable to Treasury Board for attaining federal objectives for official languages in the museums.

June 22, 1989
Museums
However, section 4 of the Memorandum of Agreement, signed by the Museums and Treasury Board with all the requisite flourishes, provides, and I quote:
If the National Museums of Canada Corporation is dismantled while the Memorandum is in effect, museum directors have the option of maintaining the Memorandum of Agreement, amending it through negotiations or signing a new agreement with Treasury Board.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit this is of special interest to me as the official languages spokesman for my party, and I am looking forward to seeing the results of these negotiations if and when they take place. We intend to monitor negotiations in this area and make sure that the decentralized museums, if we can use that term, implement language policies that are acceptable to all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the other topic which is of some interest to me is the question of marketing these museums.
As Hon. Members would know, the national museums are a basic facet of our community's cultural development because they are the repository of the collective wealth of our people. Whether we talk about founding nations, native people or New Canadians, our museums mirror the history from which future generations will draw inspiration. This is why they ought to accommodate as many visitors as possible and display the exhibits likely to attract them.
Last December 231 wrote to the National Museums of Canada Secretary-General to suggest that a tourist passport be issued, something likely to interest a great many visitors because it would open the doors to all museums without the need to pay an entrance fee. It might also enable NMC management to put some of the less popular museums on a sounder financial footing and, I am sure, make museum tours somewhat less expensive for visiting families.
My contention was that lower entrance fees through a tourist passport giving access to all museums might be implemented. I was glad to learn that the secretary responded by saying that the matter would be considered!
Just recently I got a letter from the head of the National Capital Commission in which she stated that she had endorsed the suggestion and that a tourist passport would be available to gain access to museums
and other National Capital Region institutions, and perhaps to historic sites and other points of interest to visitors.

Our museums are sometimes our best kept secrets. When I refer to the marketing principle, I refer to a method by which our museums are promoted for Canadians to visit and appreciate. While we welcome the revamping of the national museums structure, we need to ensure that more Canadians are aware of then-existence. There should be a good marketing plan to encourage tourism by making the airlines, railway and the media more interested in promoting the great contribution that our Canadian museums can make.
One year ago the Government issued a discussion paper on policy for all museums. This document described the status of museums across Canada in the dawning of the 21st century, and encouraged all interested parties to hold relevant discussions on the future of museological institutions. However, that policy lies dormant in the Department of Communications.
This new policy is needed to revitalize the non-federal museums across Canada, permitting more public programs, exhibitions of Canada's heritage and culture, and conservation of collections. It will make a greater appreciation of Canadian culture available to all regions of our land.
The Government should address this policy of marketing very soon. Our national museums are a source of Canadian heritage, culture and pride. They are a visitor's delight and they enrich our national capital. They make Canadians proud of the capital.
John Edwards, the secretary-general of National Museums of Canada did a good job and I congratulate him on his work in restructuring the museums. I hope Mr. Edwards goes on to his just rewards and I wish him continued success in his career, but I hope that every museum, independent as it will be, will make sure that Canadians, be they French or English, receive adequate service in their language on an active basis. It should be a policy of all museums to offer that service on an active basis.
Second, the Government must address the question of marketing. I hope it sees fit to introduce a good policy on marketing that will make our museums much more
June 22, 1989

interesting and encourage many more Canadians to see them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few comments on this Bill. I am pleased also that the Minister is in the House and I hope he will take note of the comments made by Members in the House today about the importance of the museums they have in their ridings as well as the museums here in Ottawa.
Our Party supports in principle the legislation which would provide the museums with a mandate that makes them more independent.
As a Member from British Columbia, I have lived quite far from the nation's capital. Since coming to Ottawa I have had a chance to tour a couple of the museums. Of course, I look forward to the opening of the new museum next week.
I took my mother through the new art gallery and, while she did not think all of it was art, we all have open minds about what is art and appreciate the importance of cultural development in this country through our museums.
I want to expand somewhat on the comments about museum policy made by my colleague, the Member for Mission-Coquitlam (Ms. Langan). One particular area that I am interested in is the need for a policy to clearly state the criteria and responsibility for museums both in the capital and in many of our smaller communities. I am particularly concerned with museums in many of our small communities throughout the country, including some of the many positive initiatives that are taken in my riding. The purpose behind the co-operation between federal and provincial Governments in developing a museum policy is to preserve and understand the history of our country. That history is very important in terms of the artefacts and documents relating to our past.
I remind the Minister of the commitments made by his Government. The museum policy was recommended in September, 1986, but we do not have one yet. I am not too critical of the Government because I think the museum community would be very grateful for an indication from the Government about the direction the Government and the provinces want to take with a museum's policy.
Museums
There are a couple of museum projects in my riding. I am a member of the Prince George Railway Museum, and smaller communities like McBride and Valemount are attempting to save their historic railway stations. We are aware of the legislation regarding heritage railway stations, but it is those kinds of projects that have missed many of the opportunities which we sometimes take for granted when we go between Parliament and the wonderful buildings we have here. Some attention should be given to those in small community-sponsored museums, not necessarily in the form of large grants, but for such things as sewer, water and electricity, or a bit of landscaping. That is the kind of extra help those smaller communities need because in most cases there is considerable volunteer effort given to these projects.
I believe there was an attempt in British Columbia to sign a communications subagreement under the economic development umbrella. I wrote a letter to the Minister on that matter because that is a vehicle to develop some of the co-operative agreements and sharing of revenue that can go toward some of the museums in our province. I would encourage the Government to seriously consider taking advantage of the upcoming expiry of some of these subagreements that we have.
In closing, I want to say that the museum community and all Members of the House would look forward eagerly to a policy from the Minister. We would see from that some specific direction, I hope, in terms of the mechanics of implementing a policy like that. In particular, my message is the concern that a lot of these smaller museums and similar types of operations have across the country. I thank you very much for this opportunity to speak.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the speeches of the last two speakers for the New Democratic Party and I am commenting as my Party's Culture and Communications critic. I too am pleased to see the Minister in the House.

I hope the Minister will be able to attend Question Period.

Museums

There should be some gender balance in these positions.

Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) do not have to worry because we are just ordinary Canadians in that way.
You're short.

I also believe as I said on a number of occasions that the Canadian Government's financial commitment to museums is not up to the Minister's expectations, which I indicate on behalf of all those who are interested in Canadian museums, and that a stronger financial commitment should be made.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to join the Hon. Member for British Columbia in his suggestions. I was privileged today to officially open the Canadian Center of Caricature, which to me is a recognition of the excellence of our cartoonists throughout our history. It also testifies to the quality of the freedom of speech and freedom of thought we enjoy in Canada. In these times where the basic principles of democracy are so easily trampled, few governments found a way to honour those who make a career out of criticizing the actions of politicians in the name of freedom of speech. To that extent, it is my hope that the action taken by the Government of Canada in recognizing both the excellence of our cartoonists and the significance of their contribution to freedom of speech, will set an example for other countries to follow and that they will also honour through their cartoonists, the quality of their democracy.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to bring, through you, to the attention of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), how much I would have enjoyed being there to enjoy the caricatures. Unfortunately the orderly disorganization of the House today has kept me here. I hope that we can finish this Bill and see the museums Bill go to a legislative committee.
I would also like to suggest that we congratulate ourselves on the development of an additional museum which will bring great joy and pleasure and I hope a lot of fun as we poke fun at each other in good sense and good judgment here in Canada.

Motion No. 1
June 16, 1989-That Bill C-6 be amended in Clause 4 by adding immediately after line 32 at page 9 the following:
"7.(1) The Governor in Council shall make regulations to require that radio authorizations may not be issued and renewals of radio authorizations may not be granted to applicants of the classes described in subsection (2).

June 22, 1989
Radio Act
whatever, by or on behalf of any persons, body, or authority of a class described in subsection (3), the corporation shall be deemed not to be an eligible Canadian corporation.
(4)	Notwithstanding subsection (3), a corporation that is
(a)	one to which paragraphs (3)(a) to (c) apply, and

(5)	With respect to any shares of a corporation of a particular class that, according to the relevant records that the corporation is required to keep under the law of the place of its incorporation, are held by individuals each of whom holds one per cent or less of the total number of issued shares of the corporation of that class, the Governor in Council may, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, accept as evidence that such shares are beneficially owned by Canadian citizens, a statement signed by the president, secretary or treasurer of the corporation, or by any other officer or persons thereunto duly authorized by the board of directors or other governing body of the corporation, indicating
(a)	that according to those records the individuals who hold the shares are individuals having addresses in Canada; and
(b)	that the persons by whom the statement is signed has no knowledge or reason to believe that the shares are not beneficially owned by Canadian citizens.
(6)	An applicant for the renewal of a radio authorization that was outstanding as of the date of the enactment of this section may not be granted such renewal, but by virtue of this section shall be deemed, for the purposes of that application only, not to be an applicant of a class described in subsection (2) if the Governor in Council is satisfied that it would not be contrary to the public interest to grant the renewal applied for by the applicant.

She said: Mr. Speaker, my amendment to Bill C-6 comes out of a deep concern for Canadian control of our communications and cultural industry, particularly with the changing economic environment and international investment patterns which we are witnessing in today's global society. Whether from Europe, Japan, or the United States those investment patterns are very significant, and I suggest that they must be taken into consideration.
Foreign investment in this country should contribute to economic growth rather than to any kind of control of our cultural industries. That was the thrust of the Free Trade Agreement, that we would not touch our cultural industries, and that goes for any other country which wants to come in here, not only the United States.
We have learned the hard lesson. Some 97 per cent of our film industry is foreign controlled, 75 per cent of our domestic book industry is foreign controlled, and 71 per cent of our periodical market consists of imported foreign product. Some 85 per cent of our domestic sales of records and tapes manufactured here in Canada come from imported master tapes. We do not control, as we should, the levers of our economic power that are found in the cultural industries. If we do not control our cultural industries and our telecommunication industries, what will continue to define us as a people?
We have just finished debating the museums Bill. That indicates that we have an historical record. Let us ensure that we have an historical record in the future that is ours, not brought in from the outside.
We do not want a repetition of these foreign ownership realities. Presently Canadians control 80 per cent of their telecommunications and broadcasting industries. This amendment would ensure that we maintain this level of control of these industries. Furthermore, it brings transparency and openness to the Government of the country and it allows for fairness of opportunity. It would require, by law, that those who acquire any radio authorization, that is any licences, be 80 per cent owned and effectively controlled by Canadians.
June 22, 1989

For example, this would require that those who hold licences for cellular telephone networks, microwave links, radio relay stations, paging transmitters, mobile data systems, air and marine radar systems, satellite communications, and citizen band radios would have to be 80 per cent Canadian owned and controlled.
This is a very normal request and a consideration of importance. In this new era of evolving technology the use of our precious commodity, that is spectrum and ownership, must be conserved in Canadian hands. It is part of the infrastructure of Canadian communication strategy. Others may use our facilities or rent our facilities, but they should not and may not own those facilities. I think that is the least that we as Canadians owe ourselves.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications has indicated that ownership of the Canadian communications infrastructure is an important issue. The Bill contains a general enabling power which gives the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations prescribing the eligibility of those who may hold certain kinds of radio licences. These eligibility criteria could include citizenship, ownership or make-up of the board of directors.
It is precisely these issues, that of controlling the eligibility by Governor in Council regulations, that concern me. The process by its very nature is secretive. It is hidden. It leaves many to wonder at times whose agenda is being served. It potentially does not provide all interested players, Canadians, in the game with the same opportunities or with clear rules, and it can allow for manipulation.
By placing ownership requirements in legislation the rules are very clear and, if the rules are to be changed, the process is open and transparent for all. That is why we are here, to legislate the kind of Canada that we want to maintain now and ensure for tomorrow in charge of its telecommunications and cultural industries that include the needed infrastructure found under the management of the Radio Telecommunications Act.
This amendment is modelled from a direction to the CRTC by the Governor in Council under the provisions of Section 22 of the 1968 Broadcasting Act.
The direction we can see in this motion is relatively complex but very precise. It includes as basic require-
Radio Act
ments that broadcasting undertakings be 80 per cent Canadian owned and effectively controlled. This direction resulted in a number of divestitures and today all broadcast undertakings, whether cable or television, are Canadian owned and controlled.
I think that we have achieved a goal of significance. The reason I bring forward this amendment is to ensure that all radio communications infrastructures are so protected through the legislative process rather than through the discretionary use of regulations and Governor in Council directives. This country has enough regulation; this country has enough Governor in Council rights. I think it is time we put into legislation the will of the people, and the will of the people is that we control our cultural levers, our telecommunications levers, and ensure that they are in Canadian hands.
This view has been supported by the task force on broadcast policy which the Minister put in place. The Caplan-Sauvageau task force made it very clear that 80 per cent ownership at minimum must be maintained. As well, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, in its sixth report in May of 1987, Legislative Provisions for New Broadcasting Legislation, made a unanimous recommendation that the key components of what constitutes ownership and effective control, that is 80 per cent owned and effectively controlled by Canadians, be written into new broadcasting legislation.
When the Minister considers bringing broadcast legislation into this House, as he might consider bringing in telecommunications legislation, as he is now revising radio communications after so many years, he must ensure that his vision and the vision that we legislators have for Canada is ownership and control of these sectors. That is what defines who and what we are. No one should control it but Canadians. Anyone else is welcome to rent it, to borrow it, to use it, but never to own it or to control it. I hope that has been made very clear. I would like to have it written into the legislation.
Therefore, I believe that this concept is a logical step for the Radio Communications Act which we are studying right now. I suggest that the cabinet direction to the CRTC, which I have had examined by legal counsel and have had adapted to suit the contents of the Radio Telecommunications Act, has a solid and proven record. It is for these reasons that I believe that this House should give its support to this amendment.

June 22, 1989
Radio Act
This is the first opportunity for the Government, since free trade and the big argument that culture was not on the table, to indicate clearly and unequivocally that culture, cultural industries, and anything else that touches that aspect of our lives are going to be owned and controlled by Canadians, whether through free trade or any other mechanism or market looking for a place to put their money. I would ask Canadians to flex their muscles for now and for tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say briefly on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we would support this amendment in that, as the Member said who presented it, the amendment would give regulating power so that these institutions could remain Canadian.
I just want to take up one thing which the Member said about whether culture and Canadianization were on the table at the free trade talks. The Government said that they were not. Of course they were. The film Bill, which was withdrawn basically at the request of the Americans, was a good example.
Last night, the Minister and I and various other people went to see a movie called Jesus of Montreal. It is a great film. One of the big problems is that it will not be seen by most Canadians because, as the member of the Liberal Party said, 97 per cent of film distribution is controlled by foreigners, mainly Americans. This is a great tragedy. We cannot see our own films in this country.
The Government has to have the guts to enact a film Bill with real teeth in it. I would be less than human if I did not suggest my own Private Members' Bill, which was the Government's original Bill. It would put some teeth and guarantee a slice of the market for Canadians. Of course, the Government cannot do that because it has signed a free deal deal with the United States. That will harmonize our industries and there will be non-discrimination clauses. The Government is stuck. It cannot do anything. It is going to Americanize Canada.
That is a longer debate. It is a debate I have consistently put before this House. I am glad the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) has now taken up the debate and mentioned all these statistics about how many of our cultural institutions remain essentially in
foreign hands. No country in the world can exist independent, like that. We have fought and struggled in this country to have an independent Francophone culture and an independent Anglophone culture. So far as this amendment assists in that grand battle for freedom and independence of Canadian culture, we will support it.

Mr. Speaker, my two hon. colleagues stated their proposed amendments very eloquently. I am sure there is a great deal of validity and the points they made are very intelligent. But under the circumstances, we believe that this amendment goes too far and would be neither practical nor useful. The Government still believes that it is better for the regulations to have the flexibility required to meet my colleagues' laudable objectives, Mr. Speaker, so that we must refuse these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, if there were not such time constraints, I would have wished the Minister would have been a little more forthcoming on the reasons why he could not accept the first amendment.

With respect to the second amendment, it is a pretty straightforward, simple one. I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, about the potential for erratic mail service. My amendment essentially states that if you are going to mail me a summons or a ticket that is going to cost me money because I supposedly broke a law, I at least ought to be entitled to a registered letter. That is what I am saying. I just bring to the Hon. Members' attention that Mr. Jim Bennett, the General Manager of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which represents 80,000 medium and small companies, calls these claims of wonderful productivity and fine new delivery performances on the part of Canada Post a little, hollow victory.

If I am going to get a ticket because I have broken a law, which is what the Government has provided in this Bill, I would suggest that the Minister consider-and Motion No. 3 is just a consequential amendment-under the offences listed on page 11 of the Bill, where it can have very serious consequences both on business and on the individual who buys a product or uses a product, the least the person is entitled to is that the information may be laid after the ticket is delivered or mailed. Let us make sure that it gets mailed in an efficient manner. My recommendation for the amendment in a simple word is: "registered mail". With that, I leave it for the Minister to comment.

Mr. Speaker, again, we believe that those are excellent suggestions. But the Government believes that it would be too restrictive to specify "registered mail" in the legislation, thus implicitly forbidding all other types of certified mail.
