Mr. Speaker, this is the first major revision of the Radio Act in 50 years. This is an instrument which the Department of Communications uses to promote the use and orderly efficient development of radio communications in Canada. In this regard, the Department has three principal regulatory functions: first, planning and standards devel-

June 22, 1989
Radio Act
opment; second, licensing of radio apparatus; and third, enforcement.
Through this legislation interference is controlled as well as the maximum number of users. In addition, it assures users access to the radio frequency spectrum and to all the benefits of radio communications. While Bill C-6 is technical and essentially a regulatory Bill, it goes far beyond a technical systems oriented approach because of whom and what it affects. It is directed primarily to the benefit of the individual in the home or at business. It impacts upon some rather common place devices which everyone takes for granted but which, in fact, only perform properly when they conform to the necessary regulations. Here I am speaking about everyday items such as the radio, television, and telephone to name just a few.
One principle of this Bill is to promote access and enable any individual to enjoy all the benefits of communications technology without one technology interfering with or reducing the benefits from another technology. That sounds pretty fundamental, but it makes sure all things work on their own and in an environment filled with other technologies. It is the kind of thing one has to explain to children and to adults. Although technology and terminology is very complex, it does have a role to play in our lives. What we are dealing with today is very important. It sets out the administrative rights and remedies which enable us to use the system.
In practical terms this legislation permits the Department of Communications to set technical standards where necessary for manufacturers, importers, and distributors of radio equipment to ensure consumers obtain safe and trouble free equipment.
The 1938 Act only allows the Department to act if it finds substandard radio equipment actually being used. Under Bill C-6, the Government will be able to stop the importation, manufacture or sale of substandard equipment. This new power will match regulations in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.
Buyers of radio equipment will not be the only consumers to benefit from the new Bill. The Bill for the first time deals with electro-magnetic immunity, the ability of radio and non-radio electronic devices to reject
unwanted radio signals and to operate normally in their presence. This is an important change as radio signals can cause malfunctions in such non-radio electronic equipment as heart pacemakers, railway crossing gates, computers, and stereos. We have all heard about viruses. The change is vital and key in terms of what has to be done.
Finally, it is with a great deal of regret that the bureaucratic input has prevented the Minister from using what I consider would have been his good judgment. He would acknowledge that to ensure 80 per cent ownership and control would only have made good sense now for his children, my children, and our grandchildren. It would have prevented for Canadians the kind of history lesson that we have in all the other cultural industries I outlined at report stage of this Bill.
I am really distressed that the Minister was not allowed to use his ministerial discretion in this instance. From my point of view the ability to ensure fairness, openness and to reduce the amount of regulatory procedures by Governor in Council would have been in the interests of all Canadians.
Although I welcome the presence of the chairman of our standing committee who should have influenced the Minister, it is with the deepest regret that I see what the Minister was unable to do because of the bureaucrats.
I have three more minutes.
Oh, oh!
Don't die, the Bill is going to the Senate. You have been rushing me all morning. I am going to have my last say. Ian, are you speaking?
Yes.
I will give him one minute, Mr. Speaker.
Oh, oh!

To ensuring fairness and due process, the Minister said no. To ensuring openness and transparency in government, the Government said no. To saying yes to Canadians and to 80 per cent Canadian ownership cent, the Minister said no. I regret all that. That is what we have. The Bill has to go, and off we go.

Oh, oh!
June 22, 1989
Mr. Speaker, that last minute and a half was the best speech I have ever heard from the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!
The Member should put herself under that deadline more often. I am glad she is allowing me to speak for one minute. She said that I could speak for a minute. I would hate to be one of her children.
They are well bred and well read children.
They must get fairly tough discipline.
Oh, oh!
I am sorry. I said "children", not grandchildren.
I have those, too.
That is nice to know. I would never have suspected that.
Oh, oh!

Before I put my foot in my mouth, I had better finish off.
On behalf of the New Democratic Party, we are agreed to the passage of this Bill. It is long overdue. We have to update technologically ourselves.
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal mentioned heart pacemakers, computers, and so on. I, too, wish that there would be more measures to protect Canadian culture, which I think is in great need of further protection if we are to develop and remain independent as a country. That has to be in another Bill and another place. I hope the Minister will bring the Broadcasting Act back soon to the House.
This afternoon?

Not this afternoon, but in the fall. Again we can see that expression of the Minister's commitment to Canadian culture, arts, cultural institutions, and CBC if I dare say that, as well as to the CRTC, and so on. We will look at the Bill to see how much the Minister has changed, to see whether he is still committed to those institutions.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to take a moment to thank all who participated in the debate in this House and in the committees and all who worked on drafting this legislation with the Department of Communications, in many consultative meetings. In closing, I would like to emphasize the importance of the spectrum management group in the Department. Although it is important, it often does not receive the publicity or discussion that other groups in the Department have, as in the cultural field, for example.
I wish to thank them for their day-to-day work to provide Canada with a very efficient spectrum management service, for the benefit of all Canadians.

Motion agreed, Bill read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, the most toxic poison with which we have managed to foul the environment are dioxins. Their elimination from all sources should be an urgent priority of this Government.
We are threatened by dioxin producing industries such as the Woodfibre pulp and paper mill in Howe Sound. However, what does the Government do in this case? It closes the fisheries, not the polluting mill. The Government chooses to deal with symptoms, not causes.
Yes, the Minister has promised tough regulations on dioxins, but not coming into force until 1990. In the meantime, why does the Minister not use the powers he has and issue an interim order to apply the regulations immediately? The cause of the problem lies with the pulp and paper mills. They should be closed, not the fisheries. To protect fisheries, the Minister must deal swiftly with pulp and paper mill pollution.

June 22, 1989
If Canadians are to take seriously the proclamation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on sustainable development, the Minister must act, for actions speak louder than words.

Mr. Speaker, a Canadian Government delegation in Geneva is being accused by native groups from several countries of attempting to undermine an international covenant on native rights.
The 150-nation International Labour Organization, a UN affiliate, is currently meeting to revise its Convention 107 on the rights of indigenous peoples, originally passed in 1957 and now considered outdated. A number of fhe amendments presented by the Canadian Government are objectionable. Native leaders are objecting more precisely to 25 amendments proposed by Canada because they believe they weaken attempts for a strong statement in the revised convention.
In view of Canada's image as a promoter of human rights, surely the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) should review this situation and instruct the head of the Canadian delegation to changes these unacceptable amendments.

Mr. Speaker, on Thes-day, June 20,1 witnessed the profound effect the recent tragic events in Beijing have had on young Canadians when I met with teacher Miriam Smith and her grade 5 class at Raymer Wood Public School in Markham. It is been an especially difficult time for some of the students who have relatives living in China.
The following are excerpts from some of the letters the students wrote as a class project to Chinese Ambassador Zhang Wenpu deploring his Government's actions in Tiananmen Square.
Christopher Reid wrote:
What is your government doing ordering your army to attack innocent people?-all they want is to discuss democracy with the government.
liana Shamoon's letter read:
-the people just wanted a discussion-it wasn't right for him (Mr. Xiaoping) to have them killed.
Anthony Latchman wrote:
I can't believe that your government said to kill people. The students weren't even armed.
Renee Pecham expressed the hope of everyone when she said:
I hope Mr. Xiaoping will come to his senses.
These young students, although 10 and 11 years of age, have come to realize the democratic system we so freely enjoy here in Canada should not be taken for granted but should be cherished and nourished.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), hides behind the constitutionality question to say that he cannot make the new sales tax visible to Canadians. I see today that constitutional experts are saying that that is nonsense.
Who should we believe? Should we believe the Minister of Finance? He said he would remove the personal surtax, but now he will not. He said he will keep the tax revenue neutral but now he will not. Finally, he said he would make the tax visible to Canadians so that everyone would know exactly how much tax they are paying, but now he will not.
Why should we trust the Minister of Finance? Does he know what it is like to have to worry about the extra $10 or $20 it will take under his new sales tax to buy a new winter coat? The Minister should withdraw his plans for the new sales tax and bury this burden in a black hole where average Canadians would like to see it go.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that Canadians are looking for better ways of dealing with the problems of rail passenger service. The Opposition seems to endorse permanently subsidizing a losing operation. The Government advocates starving

the public monopoly to death while VIA Rail bureaucrats dither over how to ration out their dwindling supplies of cash.
This week in Yellowhead, Preston Manning unveiled the Reform Party's alternative to this situation. Transport Canada should, in consultation with affected communities and labour organizations, prepare public "request for proposals" for operation of rail passenger service on a line-by-line basis. These would be solicited from potential alternative operators including VIA Rail. Contracts would be awarded to the respondent capable of doing the best job most cost effectively. This would be a formal process, free from political interference or political connections.
I would be happy to provide additional information to anyone who is interested.

Mr. Speaker, as a French-speaking Quebec Member of this House, I will have the great pleasure of sharing with my fellow Quebecers the Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day's celebrations.
Yet, this year, I will take part in these celebrations with a touch of concern in my soul. With the Meech Lake Accord, the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, had given back to us, Quebec men and women, a feeling of great pride and satisfaction because he had secured from all provincial premiers the recognition that Quebec was indeed a distinct society.
Now, we feel that this recognition to the effect that we, as Quebecers, are equal although somewhat different as partners, is shifting away from us. Some potential party leaders are even trying to reach the top at Quebeckers' expense.
While the last two undecided provinces still have almost a year to recognize this fact, let me remind you that although a federation is built on compromise, do not ask Quebec men and women to renounce their identity!

S. O. 31 FRANCE BICENTENARY OF REVOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians join with their cousins to celebrate the 200th Anniversary of the French Revolution.
Without it, Mr. Speaker, the evolution of Mankind would have been different. We would not have understood the thirst for freedom of these young Chinese in Beijing, if France had not been the first to abolish racial, religious and social discriminations.
We want the whole world to know that the efforts made by the revolutionaries who stormed the Bastille prison, and by the legislators who worked during the States General to ensure the triumph of the ideal of equality, liberty and brotherhood were not in vain.
Mr. Speaker, we continue this fight and come in a not so distant future, we shall overcome.
I therefore ask the House and all Canadians to join with me in wishing the whole French nation a happy 200th Anniversary!

Mr. Speaker, the interest free aspect of the advance payments program has been eliminated. A representative of Agriculture Canada reported to producers at a recent meeting on Prince Edward Island that a producer group in western Canada advised the Minister that advance payments impeded the marketing of canola. Out of concern, the Minister axed the program.
This same producer group has advised that it never made representation to the Minister, that its markets were not affected by advance payments and that advance payments actually complemented their marketing efforts. I submit that the excuses Island producers were given are invalid. I further submit that American demands for subsidy free agriculture in Canada are the hidden reasons behind the removal of this program. It seems that the Minister is more concerned with pleasing his American counterparts than with pleasing Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women told a family violence conference yesterday that a change in attitudes would stop family violence and that transition homes were not the answer. This sounds remarkably like a justification for why the Government is spending only $10 per year per battered woman. It is waiting for a change in attitudes so that the problem will go away.
Of course attitudes must change, but the Minister knows that one out of two battered women coming to a transition home is turned away because of lack of space. Battered women cannot afford to wait around for attitudes to change as the Government is doing. Battered women need support and services and they need them now.

ST. JEAN BAPTISTE TRIBUTES TO FRENCH CANADIANS

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity at this time-we obviously won't be sitting tomorrow-to say that June 24 is a very important holiday for us French-Canadians throughout Canada.
For us, St. Jean Baptiste Day speaks of our pride in belonging to the two great founding people of this country. For a number of years, we have taken this opportunity to raise our profile in this great country of ours.
I would also like to wish a happy holiday to all French-speaking Canadians. June 24 is a significant day and we have a reason to be proud. Together, we will celebrate throughout the country a holiday which marks our presence in North America for over 300 years. We are here to stay!

maintopic: REQUEST FOR BAN ON PHARMACIES SELLING TOBACCO PRODUCTS
REQUEST FOR BAN ON PHARMACIES SELLING TOBACCO PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a recent full-page ad sponsored by Physicians for a Smoke-free Canada reads: "Tobacco kills, smoking is a major cause of disease, disability and the premature death of 35,000 Canadians a year". This is quite true. Then the ad asks people to boycott those pharmacies that sell tobacco products. As well, the Canadian Medical Association last month asked its 46,000 members to send patients to smoke-free pharmacies.
The goal of smoke-free pharmacies is a noble one, and many across Canada have already removed tobacco from shelves. However, the Canadian Medical Association policy is totally inappropriate as long as it says nothing to patients who go to doctors who smoke. I submit that consulting a doctor who smokes is more a contradiction to good health than is buying a product in a drug store that sells tobacco.
I will accept the Canadian Medical Association boycott only after all 46,000 Canadian physicians are non-smokers.

Mr. Speaker, in Nova Scotia the allocation of social assistance is the responsibility of the municipalities. Recently, the Halifax City Manager has proposed cuts in the amounts and eligibility for assistance. For example, it will deny the working poor, unemployed with no children, and some single parents basic assistance for food, clothing, and shelter after three or four months; it will deny all special needs assistance to the disabled, single parents, and the elderly; it will deny all special needs except prescription drugs; and it will cut shelter allowance by $50 per month.
The reneging on promised child care funding allocation by the federal Government leaves many parents unable to work because of the lack of adequate, affordable child care. The federal Government has a responsi-
June 22, 1989

bility to ensure that its commitments to child care are met, that the obligations of the Canada Assistance Plan are enforced, and that the poor and the disabled in Halifax and in other Canadian communities are not abandoned in the name of deficit reduction.

Mr. Speaker, this week the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Dick) launched his Department's new and dynamic supplier relations promotion program. He also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Chairman of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Roger Hamel, under which both parties agree to work together to keep the industry better informed of how to sell to the federal Government.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce is a network of local Chambers of Commerce and of business and professional associations. It represents over 170,000 members. Mr. Speaker, that excellent program is going to give the industry easier and faster access to Government contracts.

Mr. Speaker, just over one year ago, the Communications Minister of the day announced that the postal subsidies program would remain unchanged for the next five years.
James Warrilow, President of MacLean-Hunter, said that this announcement ended the uncertainty plaguing the publishing industry. He stated that publishers would be able to plan their distribution costs for the next five years.
However, the recent Budget announced the intention of the Government to reduce postal subsidies by $10 million during 1989-90, and by $45 million each subsequent year.
These measures pose a direct threat to the publication of research and other scholarly works. The Social Science Federation of Canada indicates that this will grievously undermine the dissemination of scholarly publications in Canada.
On behalf of this organization, and the 14,000 researchers who belong to more than 65 post-secondary educational institutions across this country, I call on the Minister to renounce these restrictions on postal subsidies.
This Government should live up to its previous five-year commitment.

subtopic: THANKS TO THE MEMBERS OF THE CANADIAN ARMED

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: THANKS TO THE MEMBERS OF THE CANADIAN ARMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, National Armed Forces Day will be celebrated on June 24. Several bases and stations across the country will open their gates to the public for the occasion. There will be concerts and parades. I encourage all Canadians to visit these military facilities and to meet the men and women who work there.
Once a year, on National Armed Forces Day, we give Canadians the opportunity to thank members of the armed forces who represent us with such distinction in Canada and all over the world. They also work to protect Canada's security and sovereignty. In cooperation with our allies, they help maintain world peace. We are proud of our armed forces and we want to thank them for a job well done.

Mr. Speaker, from 1957 to 1963, the riding in the west end of Montreal named Notre-Dame-de-Grace, was represented in the House of Commons by the Hon. William "Bill" Hamilton. He was an exemplary political campaigner, visiting bus and streetcar stops early and late, and in all weather conditions to meet his electors. As a young Conservative, I was proud to work on his enthusiastic campaign team.

June 22, 1989
Oral Questions
He served admirably as Postmaster General in the Government of Prime Minister Diefenbaker, and as a business leader in Vancouver. He became a member of the Macdonald Royal Commission that studied Canada's economic future.
Following his recent death at 70, all Canadians join with his family in celebrating a life of service, and expressing thanks to Bill Hamilton.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter which I believe is of concern to all Members of the House.
A deduction due to a disability is something that has been in place for a number of years in our tax system. However, the Government has set up a system which makes it extremely difficult for individuals to qualify, and could lead to discouraging people from applying for this very legitimate deduction.
The Government has set up a disability determination section in Ottawa to make decisions on the claims local Revenue Canada officers do not feel are clear-cut. However, I have a large number of files in my office of individuals, some of whom have been waiting a year or more to obtain a ruling on their deduction for disability. When one calls the local Revenue Canada office, it will not give the number for the disability determination office in Ottawa. When I called the Department of National Revenue in Ottawa, a member of the Minister's departmental staff had not even heard of such an office.
I do not think that it is legitimate for Revenue Canada to expect people to wait for a year or more before receiving an answer, thus causing disabled individuals increased stress and anxiety. I urge the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Jelinek) to move immediately to put some speed into this snail-like system and stop penalizing the less fortunate members of our society.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Contrary to his earlier and repeated assurances that the new federal sales tax would be plainly visible to all consumers, the Minister has stated that the Government has now learned that it does not have the constitutional right to make it clear to consumers how much tax they are actually paying.
Yesterday, among others, the Minister of Finance for Saskatchewan stated: "Our constitutional people strongly disagree with that. It is our view that he, the federal Minister of Finance, does have that power".
Would the Minister now state clearly, whose constitutional advice he took, and how he arrived at his remarkable conclusion? Will he table a statement indicating how the Constitution limits the ways in which a federal tax is administered, including the procedures necessary to make it clear at the cash register what sales tax consumers are actually paying?

Mr. Speaker, one of the principal motives of the Government in sales tax reform is to make it much clearer than it is under the existing sales tax system precisely what amount of sales tax consumers are paying.
Under the proposed system, the goods and services tax, we will be bringing the sales tax to the retail level in order that everyone will know that on taxable goods, they pay 9 per cent tax at the retail level. As I indicated yesterday, that is simply not the case today. People do not know what federal sales tax they are paying. Under the goods and services tax we are taking a major step forward in the awareness that consumers will have of the existing tax.
The Hon. Member asks if we have the legal right to do this. Our legal advice is that we do not have the legal right to require a retailer to impose the tax extra to pricing, or to include it in the pricing. That is an option for the consumer.
June 22, 1989

Under the technical paper that we will be making available shortly, it will show very clearly how the federal Government will encourage the much greater awareness of consumers of the sales tax that they are paying.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has indicated that the greater visibility that he has promised will be in the form of a small sign that will hang in a shop indicating that sales tax will be paid on some or all of the products sold in that shop. In failing to ensure that the new federal sales tax will be clearly visible, he is leaving the provinces with no alternative but to collect their provincial sales tax on top of the federal sales tax. This double taxation will give the provinces a windfall of almost a half billion dollars of taxpayers' money.
Will the Minister now keep his promise to Canadians by taking immediate steps to ensure that the new federal sales tax will be added at the cash register, as it should be, so that one tax is not being piled on top of another tax?

Mr. Speaker, let me expand on my comment which I gave in answer to the first question to illustrate the point that I made.
A study done of the 12 per cent rate-and not the 13.5 per cent rate that is in place right now-shows that the highest effective tax rate at the retail level is 12.67 per cent. Under the same tax the lowest effective tax rate is 6.05 per cent. The consumer does not know whether it is 12.67 per cent or 6.05 per cent, or anything in between.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: And he still won't know.

The Hon. Member says that he still will not know. He will know that on that product there will be a 9 per cent tax regardless of where he buys it, who he buys it from and what the brand name is. It will be 9 per cent and it will be very clear to Canadians that it will be 9 per cent.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows perfectly well that under his present
Oral Questions
plan a consumer shopping in a supermarket will pay tax on certain items in that supermarket and not on other items. He knows perfectly well that that will confuse and obfuscate the collection of taxes at the retail point.
The Minister has promised that the new tax will be clearly visible. It will not be. He promised that it will be revenue neutral. He knows that it will not be. He promised that surtaxes on income tax will be removed when the new tax is introduced. He knows that they will not be.
Can the Minister now assure the House that the substantial tax credits, which he has promised continually to the Canadian people to offset the regressive nature of the new tax, will be in place and will be of a character to ensure that the poorer people in our society are not paying an undue amount of this tax?

Mr. Speaker, I have indicated very clearly on a number of occasions that answers to questions related to the awareness of consumers of the tax, the impact on our revenue position, the impact on low-income people and the benefits to be gained from the refundable sales tax credit will all be very clear when we make available the technical paper.
The important point that needs to be made here is that what the Hon. Member is saying about the hidden nature of the existing tax underscores quite clearly the reasons why we have to move to a new sales tax system and why his Party-and I believe he himself-has supported the fact that we must change from the existing sales tax system to the new sales tax system. I appreciate the support of the Liberal Party of Canada to moving forward to the goods and services tax.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AIR INDIA FLIGHT 181-INVESTIGATIONS OF CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, four years ago tomorrow, on June 23, 1985, Air India flight 181 en route from Toronto to London was bombed before it reached London. Some 329 people were murdered, most of them were Canadians.

June 22, 1989
Oral Questions
The Canadian Government has bungled the investigation from day one. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police was involved with erased tapes. The Canadian Security Intelligence Service has also been involved in some false affidavits.
Today, a new book alleges that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has been investigating and, in fact, investigating at length a link between agents of the Indian Government and the bombing.
I would like to put my question to the Prime Minister. Is he aware of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service investigating this link?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: AIR INDIA FLIGHT 181-INVESTIGATIONS OF CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand why my colleague asks the question, in view of the long delay. But I believe that I already informed the House several weeks ago that the RCMP is still conducting a criminal investigation. The Commissioner informed me about it.
You know all that is involved in this affair, Mr. Speaker, and any further statement at this time, while criminal investigations are underway and civil cases are before the courts-Unfortunately, I feel it is completely inappropriate at this stage to comment further any way whatsoever on this case, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ROYAL COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
REQUEST FOR ROYAL COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is nonsense. For four years we have been told the same story. Time and time again the Government of Canada says that the investigation is ongoing and charges are imminent.
We have had a royal commission of inquiry in Canada into the conduct of a Cabinet Minister, Sinclair Stevens. Another one is going on into the conduct of an Olympic athlete. Here we have the most hideous and horrific crime ever in Canadian history. For some reason the Government of Canada refuses to initiate a royal commission of inquiry.
Is the Minister refusing to initiate a royal commission of inquiry because of the bungling of his Government, because of the false affidavits, because of the erased tapes, because of the advance warnings that the Government had? Or is it because of the link with the Indian Government?
I would like the Prime Minister to stand up. He has an obligation to the families of the victims to stand up in the House of Commons and to tell us exactly what was behind the Air India bombing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ROYAL COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these questions were raised just a few days ago in the Standing Committee. The RCMP Commissioner informed those in attendance that more than thirty RCMP officers were now working on the case. Obviously, it is most unfortunate. Many people died. This type of investigation takes a lot of time to get all the facts.
I was assured by both the RCMP Commissioner and the Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service that the two agencies cooperated and did all they could to move this investigation forward. It is making progress.
Unfortunately, it seems to me quite inappropriate to raise this issue or to bring up the investigation in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, we must let the RCMP continue this investigation. It has committed all the available energy and resources required for this purpose.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It refers to a Finance Committee report issued on monetary policy. It was issued this morning.
The Minister is now aware, of course, that we have a national consensus which includes the 10 Premiers, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the small business community, the farming community and the Finance Committee of this House which represents all three Parties, which states that interest rates must come down, and must come down now.
Hear, hear!

In light of the fact that the Finance Committee report states: "Monetary restraint can be too tough and too long" and makes the primary recommendation that the Bank of Canada must relax its stance on monetary policy now. I want to know from the Minister of Finance whether or not he agrees that enough is enough, that it is the time to act, and that he instruct
June 22, 1989

John Crow to bring down the bank rate and bring it down now.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the work that is being done by the Finance Committee can be a useful contribution to the whole discussion of monetary policy.
However, I have to draw to the attention of the Hon. Member the fact that just this week we have had an indication of the tremendous strength in the economy over the past couple of years, and the fact that we have had an upward adjustment in the amount of growth in the economy which puts Canada right at the top of major industrialized nations in economic growth over the past two years. That, together with the ongoing high levels of inflation we have also seen this past week, in face of the increased level of the Canadian dollar and the high interest rates we have been encountering over the past number of months, indicates quite clearly that the Governor of the Bank of Canada, whose position has been fully supported by the Government, has been correct in maintaining the monetary policy he has been following. If we had not followed that policy, we would have had a much more serious inflation problem.
If the Hon. Member needs to be reminded, that is what got us into the mess we had in 1981 and 1982 when we had the most serious recession this country had seen since the 1930s.
Hear, hear!
The Minister of Finance is sounding more and more like a clone of Allan MacEachen every day.
Oh, oh!
Withdraw.
How could you stoop so low?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has struck a tender cord.

I suppose I have also insulted the Senator in the other place, Mr. Speaker.
Oral Questions

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LOWERING OF BANK RATE
REQUEST FOR LOWERING OF BANK RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now eight weeks since the Minister promised in his April 26 Budget to lower the interest rate set by the Bank of Canada. Mr. Speaker, we now have the support of Opposition Members on this side and Government Members on that side for reducing the rate.
Is the Minister of Finance prepared to say this has gone far enough, to do his duty and tell John Crow the time has come to lower interest rates in Canada?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LOWERING OF BANK RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, according to the rules of the House, I believe I would have to give you notice at the earliest possible opportunity of a question of privilege after the Hon. Member's descriptions of me in his preamble. It is slanderous and I cannot accept that.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LOWERING OF BANK RATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LOWERING OF BANK RATE
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that he would like to see lower interest rates. The Government of Canada would like to see lower interest rates. We believe that we have put in place a Budget which will lead to lower interest rates. That is the position I set in the budget speech itself, as well as on a number of occasions since that time.
However, markets must be allowed to work. The Governor of the Bank of Canada cannot wave a magic wand, nor can the Minister of Finance. Markets have to work to allow interest rates to come down.
If they are brought down artificially, it will result in precisely the problems we went through in the 1970s when the Government of the day ignored the problems of inflation, which led to the mess we got into in the 1980s. That is something that we on this side of the House are determined to avoid, even though the members in the New Democratic Party are quite happy to return us to the mess we got into at that time as a country.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED NATIONAL TAX-MINISTER'S POSITION
WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED NATIONAL TAX-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows very well that one of the problems

June 22, 1989
Oral Questions
with the high bank rate has been the inflation rate, which has been created in part by the taxes of the Government opposite.
The proposed national sales tax will add at least 2.5 to 3 points to the Consumer Price Index. When the CPI goes up, Governor Crow usually responds by jacking up the interest rates.
In light of the pigheadedness of Mr. Crow, will the Minister of Finance make a commitment today to withdraw the proposal for a national sales tax, bring down interest rates, and strengthen the economy?

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED NATIONAL TAX-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume the Hon. Member is saying that he wants us to withdraw the goods and services tax and return to the hidden tax, that existing federal sales tax and all the problems it has caused. He is also turning his back totally on the tax probe of the New Democratic Party which stated that the existing sales tax is a mess.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED NATIONAL TAX-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Answer the question.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED NATIONAL TAX-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Let me address the substance of the Hon. Member's question about what will be the response of the Governor of the Bank of Canada to that short-term, one time only inflation impact.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada has indicated to me that he just does not look at the nominal numbers of inflation but at the underlying performance of the economy and what is happening to the underlying rate of inflation, to the growth and demand in the economy. He looks at what is happening to capacity utilization and monetary growth rates. All these things form monetaiy policy, not the one single item of the raw figure for inflation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Today's release of the book Soft Target reveals the elaborate and covert operations of the India Government in Canada to discredit and destabilize the Canadian
Sikh community and the manipulation of the Minister and his Department in this scheme.
Given that CSIS has confirmed to the authors that a special investigation was conducted into the behaviour of Indian diplomats in Canada, and that a report was submitted to the Minister's Department in 1986, will the Minister inform the House of the details of that report? Will he confirm or deny that he refused to act on that serious and sensitive report because he did not want to jeopardize a $1.9 billion pipeline deal between Canada and India?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I try to keep up with current literature, but I have not had the opportunity yet to read the book to which the Hon. Member is making reference. I will take a look at that. I will treat his question with the seriousness I usually accord to his questions.
Let me deal with the last implication in his question. That implication is false.

Mr. Speaker, there are also allegations in the book that officials from the Department of External Affairs knowingly got involved with the Indian Consulate in Toronto that paid informants to spy and oversee the actions of various members of that Canadian Sikh community.
Given the Minister's own track record with this community, the letter to the Premiers, the intervention in Sikh refugee cases, the attempted blocking of the Canadian chair of Sikh studies in Vancouver, and the Minister's refusal to appear before the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism to justify his actions, is the Minister concerned about this unholy matrimony between the Government of India and the Government of Canada, when the rights of Canadian citizens of Sikh origin in this country are being violated? Don't you have any respect for their citizenship in this country?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is exceeding even his low standards in some of the allegations he is making. We make Canadian policy for Canadian reasons. We place as a priority of Canadian policy the interests of Canadian citizens.
We also maintain relations with friendly Governments. If those friendly Governments engage in any activities, including intelligence activities which are inappropriate,
June 22, 1989

we deal with them directly, we reprimand them directly, and we require the removal from the country of people involved in those improper activities.
The Hon. Member should not abuse his position as an elected Member of this House of Commons to try to raise these kinds of allegations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The Minister has stated on several occasions that only 3 per cent of Canadians ride the train, but he has never gone on to say that only 4 per cent of Canadians ride the bus and that only 7 per cent travel by air, while 85 per cent of Canadians travel by automobile.
Why is the Minister so determined to run VIA off the rails rather than support the corporation as he should be doing?

Mr. Speaker, the best way to help a corporation and a country is to ensure that both the corporation's and the country's finances are in good shape. That is exactly what we want to do with VIA Rail. I did not say that 6 per cent of Canadians travel by bus because I was talking about VIA Rail and about the ridership of VIA Rail. However, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the funds allocated to VIA Rail in the last Budget reflect the frequency with which Canadians use this transport mode, and it is on the basis of this information that we intend to apply the present budgetary restrictions.

Mr. Speaker, today the Minister has said that he will use Orders in Council to slaughter VIA Rail.
Why has the Minister decided that democracy in this country no longer matters? When will he stop using the math of the Minister of Finance and the truth of the Prime Minister to deal with this House?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, what I have said, and I repeat it, is that in the budget of April 27 there are many proposals or possibilities to deal with the VIA Rail budget.
One of those proposals could be abandonment of routes. If it happens, we could consider different options. Within the options is one is to go directly, by Section 64, to Order in Council. However, it will be done when we know if there are abandonments. Until that period of time I believe it is just speculation.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister concerning Patricia Starr and the Prince Charles Housing Project in Toronto.
The Prime Minister knows the charitable status of this building depends on it being exclusively charitable in the judgment of Revenue Canada. This charitable status was only obtained with the intervention of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Can the Prime Minister explain why charitable status has been continued when such needy persons as Mrs. Starr's son and a staff member of Premier David Peterson's office were both residents of this complex?
Why are Liberal and Conservative Party connections the main requirements for tax subsidized housing at Patty's Place?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say first that the National Council of Jewish Women of Canada, the Toronto section, has co-operated fully with Revenue Canada in its ongoing investigation. I think that should be made very clear off the top.
Revenue Canada is conducting an investigation into their operations. We are having co-operation from them. I think we should wait until that investigation is finished before the Hon. Member jumps to some of the totally unfounded conclusions he has jumped to.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Prime Minister.

June 22, 1989
Oral Questions
During the 1988 election, the PC Canada Fund received $2,000 from the Starr charity for dinner for the Prime Minister.
Does the Prime Minister consider himself to be a charity worthy of a $2,000 donation for a meal?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, people buy tickets to events. If any moneys have come into the hands of the PC Canada Fund or Members of Parliament that are not rightfully there, they will be returned.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JIM DINNING, ALBERTA MINISTER OF EDUCATION

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JIM DINNING, ALBERTA MINISTER OF EDUCATION
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of Hon. Members the presence in our gallery today of the Honourable Jim Dinning, Minister of Education of the Government of Alberta.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JIM DINNING, ALBERTA MINISTER OF EDUCATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CHANGES IN THE REGULATIONS CONCERNING SEXUAL DELINQUENTS
CHANGES IN THE REGULATIONS CONCERNING SEXUAL DELINQUENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General.
According to an article which appeared this morning in the Globe and Mail, the National Parole Board Regulations will be changed to prevent the premature release of sexual offenders.
Could the Minister explain why these changes were not made before and how they will affect Bill C-67?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: CHANGES IN THE REGULATIONS CONCERNING SEXUAL DELINQUENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member said, this Government adopted Bill C-67 for the purpose of preventing dangerous criminals-this is a very important issue which affects all Canadians, Mr. Speaker.
Canadians are concerned about dangerous criminals and especially about the fact that they might be released
before serving their full sentence. There was still one major point that my predecessor submitted to a task force, namely, the severe harm that might be caused.
I asked officials in my Department, the Deputy Minister responsible for the National Parole Board and Correctional Services, to come up with a more restrictive definition of severe harm, which we did quite recently. As a result, and Canadians will be pleased to hear this, now that we have tightened up the criteria for evaluating severe harm, our system will be able to offer better protection to all Canadians. I think that is good news.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF EXPORT TAX ON LUMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, my question is for the Prime Minister. He will know that 1,300 employees at the G. W. Martin Lumber Ltd. are some of the latest victims of the Government's softwood lumber agreement which really has devastated the industry in northern Ontario.
The Minister for International Trade has said that he agrees that the export tax is unfair because of the increase in exchange rates and should be removed. Is the Prime Minister prepared to undertake that his Government will end this tax?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF EXPORT TAX ON LUMBER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is involved in consultations that we hope will allow a regime to be put in place that would remove the necessity for that tax. I am not in a position to give details on the extent of those negotiations.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF EXPORT TAX ON LUMBER
speechtext: I certainly appreciate the Minister's answer.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
The Minister for International Trade is willing to go to the GATT to have an unfair U.S. import tax on oil imports removed to help the energy sector, but he is unwilling to stand up to the Americans on the lumber issue where an unfair export tax which we are collecting is costing thousands of Canadians their jobs.
June 22, 1989

Why this double standard? Will the Prime Minister explain this sell-out of workers in northern Ontario?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no double standard. There is certainly no desire to do anything but help workers in northern Ontario and elsewhere in the country.
What is at issue here is the necessity to have in place some agreement between Canada and the United States that will take the place of a tax whose history is well known to Members of this House. Those discussions involving Canada and the United States are going forward, and there are consultations with the Canadian industries affected.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for tourism. The Minister has decided not to renew or, rather, abandon the Economic Regional Development Agreements for tourism in particular, and especially for the eastern provinces.
Every provincial Ministry of Tourism in the country has clearly indicated that the Government has no real understanding of the tourism industry, no plans, and now diminishing means to assist in a marketing strategy for the provinces.
Can the Minister explain how his Ministry is so totally at odds with every other tourist Ministry in the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the premise in the Hon. Member's question, the Government in fact is coming to terms with modem realities.
We had in the past ERDA arrangements which funded up $246 million with the provinces. They have produced a great deal of product and they have on the whole contributed largely to the regional development of those economies.
However, there were problems with the agreements. They were cumbersome. Decision making was some-
Oral Questions
times difficult. Also there was not enough emphasis on marketing instead of product development.
We are going to put a new regime in place with the regional agencies. I will, in consultation with my colleagues, bring this whole program up to modem standards rather than keep it in the old world.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CALL IN PROVINCIAL COUNTERPARTS
REQUEST THAT MINISTER CALL IN PROVINCIAL COUNTERPARTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, considering what I have heard from most tourism departments in Canada, could the Minister, before he introduces a new system, perhaps inform the House whether he intends to at least call a meeting of provincial Tourism Ministers to keep the situation from deteriorating any further?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CALL IN PROVINCIAL COUNTERPARTS

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I place before you today the third reading of Bill C-19, an amendment to the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program. The purpose of this Bill is to implement the decision announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his recent Budget to terminate CEDIP incentives on April 27, 1989, except for certain activities under way or required to be undertaken pursuant to written agreements in place as of that date.
CEDIP was created in March, 1987 as a temporary financial bridge to assist the oil and gas industry in adjusting to a precipitous decline in world oil prices. Oil prices have dropped from $30 U.S. a barrel to $10 U.S. a barrel in a very short period of time. The Government of Canada was sensitive to the disruption in the cash flow and investment caused by the rapid fall of oil prices. CEDIP was brought in to assist the industry in maintaining upstream investment and employment. It provided cash incentives to maintain exploration and development activities. The program was primarily intended to help the smaller to medium-sized companies, the part of the sector that was facing the most difficulties.
Current projections are that the program would provide $1.25 billion in assistance to the industry. The program will have supported over $3.7 billion in exploration and development activity, the bulk of it in western Canada. For 1987-1988, the first year of CEDIP and the only one for which the deadline on applications has lapsed, industry will have been provided with roughly $500 million dollars in incentives.
The decision to terminate CEDIP, I would again stress, was not an easy one. We know that the oil and gas industry is upset by the lack of notice provided on this decision. But coming to grips with our deficit problems means making difficult decisions.
The termination of CEDIP will save the Government of Canada $80 million. We have instituted grandfathering provisions in order to honour activities under way or committed to underwritten agreements. This grandfathering regime will cushion the impact of program termination. Incentives will be provided on grandfathered activities through to December 31, 1989 when the program will be completely terminated. The grandfathering will help many companies. We fully realize that by asking the oil patch to contribute $80 million toward the deficit, some companies will have more difficulty than others in adjusting their investment plans to take into account the Budget decision.
June 22, 1989

I would hope that the decisions taken will be accountable for and will help the Government of Canada in its very difficult deficit position.
At this time I would like to thank the members of the legislative committee who co-operated with the Minister and myself to ensure that we could get passage of this Bill.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great exception to this Bill because I think it will do a great deal of harm. I take great exception to the way the Department of Energy has handled this whole question. It has continued to mislead the public by refusing to state exactly how damaging this is going to be and to admit that the smaller companies for which this program was brought forward have received veiy little of the benefit of this program. Although it is a program to aid small companies, the smaller companies have received less than 15 per cent of the money. In fact, 90 per cent of the applicants under this program received less than 15 per cent of the funds. This has been substantiated by the Government's own information.
In a news release dated June 20, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources states: "The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources Monday presented detailed information to the House of Commons Legislative Committee studying the Bill to terminate the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, Bill C-19, which revealed that 56 per cent of the money available under the program went to small and medium-sized firms and applicants. CEDIP will provide $1.5 million", and so on. Then the release goes on to say that only 44 per cent will be paid to large companies.
More than 85 per cent of the funds under this program will be paid to large companies. Yet small companies are being used as a scapegoat for the cancellation of this program. If this Government reduced the ceiling from $10 million to $1 million under this program, 90 per cent of the applicants could have their applications honoured and the Government would save 65 per cent of the funds. On the one hand, the Government is saying that it will save $80 million. On the other hand, the Government is saying this program will cost $1.2 billion. Yet the Government is only saving $80 million for the rest of the
Exploration and Development
term, which would be from April 27 to the end of December this year. This would be 33 per cent of the length of the program if the program were allowed to run its complete course. Why is the Government only saving $80 million if two-thirds of the program is going to cost $1.2 billion? There has to be a very big discrepancy.
The Department is also saying that to date it has spent $663.6 million, which is half of what it proposed the program will cost. I know a lot of companies will have to file later than this particular date, but certainly half of the $1.2 billion being estimated will not be requested after the actual program is cancelled. The Government is exaggerating the cost of this program. Once again it is putting the blame on the backs of the small oil companies for something that is not their fault and it is not a program under which they will benefit to anywhere near the extent the Government is predicting.
That being the case, what is going to be the situation? We heard from some very good witnesses: the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada and the Petroleum Services Association of Canada submitted briefs. We heard some very interesting remarks and statements which all indicated that activity in the western sedimentary basin is declining at an alarming rate.
The brief presented by the Petroleum Services Association of Canada indicates that this year, 25,000 people will be involved in the service industry in the western sedimentary basin. In the last two and a half years alone, that is down from a total of between 40,000 and 45,000 workers. In two and a half years, 20,000 jobs have been lost in the service industry in the western sedimentary basin, an alarming decline in activity.
Drillers have told us that in the second quarter of 1989, there will be only 100 rigs in use. That second quarter is almost over so there is not much guesswork involved. That is down from the second quarter of last year when there were 171 rigs in operation. However, the price of oil this year is higher than it was last year. The situation is not a reflection of oil prices, it is a reflection of the fact that major companies are merging. They are getting their reserves through mergers. They are paper shuffling, not drilling or exploring. Yet the smaller companies that want to drill and explore are not able to get the funding from the banks. Now this

June 22, 1989
Exploration and Development
program is being taken away from them without any advance notice whatsoever.
The Petroleum Services Association told us that although there will be 100 rigs operating in the second quarter, they need 200 rigs for there to be any kind of profit margin for the petroleum services industry. Only 50 per cent of the rigs required for a profitable period are in operation. That is incredible.
The petroleum services industry and the drillers are also telling us that they need between 40 per cent and 60 per cent activity on the rigs, yet these 100 rigs only represent 20 per cent of the rigs that are available for use in the western sedimentary basin.
The Government would have us believe everything is hunky dory with respect to the conventional oil and gas industry. That is not true. The Government is talking about megaprojects. It is allowing and in some cases even encouraging the mergers of these companies. Yet it is walking away from one of the best employers in Canada, the conventional oil and gas industry. It is doing this without any regard whatsoever for the people involved or the companies involved. Some of the companies involved have been in business for decades, have been handed down from one generation to another. These companies are in trouble. The companies in the drilling industry and the service industry, the small explorers and developers, are the companies that are in difficulty. Jobs are continually being lost. In the last two and half years, 20,000 jobs were lost and thousands more could be lost before the end of 1989.
What has the Government done? It brought forward a program called the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, mainly for mining companies. It provides good incentives for mining companies, but because of the retroactive provisions of the exploration definition clause under the Tax Act, the oil and gas industry will not be able to take advantage of this program. A company could drill a well, find oil, receive funds under CEDIP and then have to pay those funds back later on when another well is drilled and it is determined by the Government that the well for which they got the funds was not an exploration well. Not only would the company have to repay the money but it would have to pay interest on the money received.
The Government has levelled a large corporation tax against small companies in the oil and gas sector. I think a large corporation tax has benefits and there is a need for it, but not one imposed on small companies that are not operating. These companies have to pay the tax whether they are operating or not, whether or not they are making a profit. As long as they have assets of over $10,000, they have to pay a tax. This is an asset tax which the small producers have said is much more despicable than the PGRT ever was.
Let us return to the program at hand, the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program. When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) was in Calgary on April 5, he said that this program would extend to the end of the year. On April 17 in the House of Commons he said that date would not change. Yet on April 26, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) cancelled this program immediately without any notice whatsoever, even though the Act itself contains a stipulation that any change in the rate of pay would require six months' notice. Not only was the rate of pay changed from 25 per cent to zero per cent, but the whole program was cancelled. However, no notice was given.
The small producers, drillers and those in the service industry had been planning on using this program until the end of the year. This is immoral. Just because the law allows the Government to do this, there is no way it is justified in cancelling a program without any notice when the Act says it has to give six months' notice. This is the treatment that is being given to the oil and gas sector. This is the treatment that is being given to the western sedimentary basin and to the western part of Canada when thousands of jobs are being lost.
We are losing six months of the program and I think that has to be rectified. For that reason, I would like to propose a motion. With respect to the motion for third reading of this Bill, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier):
That all the words in the motion after the word "that" be deleted,
and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill C-19, an Act to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act, be not now read a third time but that it be read a third time this day six months hence".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that there is any need for me to go into great detail about Bill C-3. We have looked at it on more than one occasion in the House. A fair amount of time was spent on it the other night at report stage.
It is an important Bill that will have a significant impact on research, science, technology, and those areas that are very important to Canadians.
